Hypothesis Bayes Factors

Source: R/hypothesis-BF.R
hypothesis_BF.Rd

Computes Bayes factors for scalar hypotheses written as expressions, for example "theta = 0", "theta > 0", or "theta = 0 vs theta > 0". hypothesis_BF() is a generic: the default method evaluates posterior draws and marginal posteriors, and the method for a fitted model (BayesTools_fit) tests the quantities of its parameter catalog by their public names (see Fitted models). Factor/posterior-list levels can be referenced as "mu_alloc[alternate] > mu_alloc[random]" when the marginal posterior carries joint prior information. Level names that contain brackets, such as the cut() level (0,1], are referenced by quoting the whole reference in backticks, "`mu[(0,1]]` > `mu[(1,2]]`", or with the parameter catalog's escaped level form mu["(0,1%5D"]. Point-null hypotheses use Savage_Dickey_BF when a marginal_posterior object is supplied, including precomputed qCMDE/IWMDE posterior ordinates when density_method = "precomputed". Level-specific marginal_posterior.* subclass vectors with attached density metadata are accepted as marginal posterior inputs; parent-level posterior_density, posterior_densities, posterior_ordinate, or posterior_ordinates metadata on a marginal-posterior list is reused for matching level hypotheses.

hypothesis_BF(posterior, ...)

# Default S3 method
hypothesis_BF(
  posterior,
  prior = NULL,
  hypothesis,
  parameter = NULL,
  logBF = FALSE,
  BF01 = FALSE,
  seed = NULL,
  density_method = c("KDE", "normal", "precomputed"),
  columns = "default",
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'BayesTools_fit'
hypothesis_BF(
  posterior,
  hypothesis,
  namespace = NULL,
  component = NULL,
  transform_scaled = FALSE,
  conditional = FALSE,
  logBF = FALSE,
  BF01 = FALSE,
  seed = NULL,
  density_method = "KDE",
  density_control = NULL,
  n_samples = 10000,
  columns = "default",
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'BayesTools_hypothesis_BF'
as.data.frame(x, row.names = NULL, optional = FALSE, ...)

Arguments

posterior

posterior draws, a marginal_posterior, a marginal_inference object, or a data frame/matrix of posterior draws, or a model fitted with JAGS_fit() (a BayesTools_fit). Posterior draws must be finite and quantity names must be unique.

...

for the cbind() method, the tables to bind; unused by the as.data.frame() method. The method for draws takes no further arguments and stops on unknown ones; the method for a fitted model warns about them.

prior

prior draws for numeric/data-frame inputs, or for numeric draws a scalar BayesTools prior object (including mixture and spike-and-slab priors). Quantity names in draw tables must be unique. Ignored when posterior already contains deterministic prior density information.

hypothesis

character vector with scalar hypothesis statements written in the restricted grammar described in Details, or, for posterior draws and marginal posteriors, a validated object from hypothesis_parse(). The method for a fitted model takes character strings only and stops with the BayesTools_hypothesis_statement condition for a parsed hypothesis.

parameter

optional scalar quantity name for numeric vectors or marginal_posterior objects.

logBF

whether to display the Bayes factor on the log scale.

BF01

whether to display the inverse Bayes factor.

seed

optional finite seed used by downstream helpers that sample. The caller's random-number generator state is restored after the call.

density_method

posterior density source for point-null tests. "KDE" uses kernel density estimates. "normal" uses a normal approximation to the posterior density at the null. "precomputed" requires valid posterior_ordinate or posterior_density metadata (posterior_metadata()) and errors if no valid precomputed source is available. KDE point-null tests use boundary reflection when exact support metadata is attached to the marginal posterior or to matched posterior_density metadata, and, for numeric draws with a prior object, at the bounds that prior object declares (its truncation, or the support of its family) when the draws lie within them; other numeric and data-frame expression tests use standard Gaussian sample KDE. For numeric draws with a prior object that declares point masses, the posterior ordinate is that of the absolutely continuous part: the share of the draws not at a declared point-mass location times the KDE of those draws. A point hypothesis on a linear expression of marginal-posterior parameters or levels (sums, differences, and constant multiples, e.g., mu[B] - mu[A] = 0; functions and powers only of constants) is tested as a Savage-Dickey ratio of that linear combination: the prior density and exact support come from the joint prior context and the posterior ordinate is the normal approximation ("normal") or the KDE with boundary reflection at bounded supports (per mixture component, see Savage_Dickey_BF). An affine expression of a numeric quantity with a prior object uses the exact density of that transformed prior. Only user-supplied prior draws use the sample KDE of the prior expression draws, with a classed warning (see Value). Finite sample and KDE evaluation ranges are not treated as exact support, so finite point hypotheses outside those ranges use kernel-tail density estimates.

columns

output columns. "default" returns Alternative, Null, BF, and BF_error. "all" also returns prior, posterior, and method columns. The prior and posterior columns are diagnostics, not always probabilities: point tests report density heights, region tests report odds, and transitive point-vs-region tests report NA. The default BF_error column is printed as error%(BF). Individual columns are selected by these column names; other spellings are rejected.

namespace, component, transform_scaled, conditional, density_control, n_samples

arguments of the method for a fitted model, passed to hypothesis_BF_model(), which documents them: the component of the model that the statements refer to (namespace: the formula parameter such as "mu", "model", or "random"), the level of a factor term that references to the term without a level stand for (component, which combines with namespace), the scale (transform_scaled = FALSE, the default, tests the fitted scale as in JAGS_estimates_table()), the conditioning of the tested quantities on their inclusion events, the settings of the density backend, and the number of prior samples.

x

a hypothesis Bayes factor table.

row.names

optional row names for the complete exported frame.

optional

logical; exported column names are always syntactic and unique.

Value

A BayesTools table of class BayesTools_hypothesis_BF. The BF_error column reports approximate relative Monte Carlo error percentage when available. Region odds errors are computed on log(BF) from prior/posterior region indicators using an iid delta-method approximation on the flattened draws; they do not adjust for MCMC autocorrelation. Prior region masses computed deterministically from a prior object's distribution function contribute no Monte Carlo error. Point-vs-region errors combine the available point-density and region-mass errors on the log(BF) scale. Point-null tests require a regular prior ordinate with finite log density at the null value that prior_density_ordinate() classifies exactly from the prior's structure, on every route. Otherwise they stop with a classed error condition, which callers should match by class rather than by message: BayesTools_point_mass_at_null (a prior point mass at the null), BayesTools_infinite_ordinate, BayesTools_zero_ordinate, BayesTools_undefined_ordinate, or BayesTools_inexact_ordinate (no exact structural ordinate, e.g., a nonlinear expression of a deterministic prior, a prior-density combination evaluated only on a numerical grid, a structural quadrature rejected by its diagnostics, or a density grid without recorded provenance). Each of these conditions also has class BayesTools_hypothesis_ordinate. For a whole-factor statement expanded into several quantities, known ordinate errors produce an NA row with method "unavailable" and the original reason; valid siblings are computed. Declared formula measure refusals of class BayesTools_formula_measure_unavailable behave likewise, preserving their original reason and diagnostics. Only the declared formula-measure cause allow-list is localized; metadata, refit, and programming errors propagate. Direct scalar and explicitly indexed tests remain strict. Known numerical prior-region errors behave likewise, with classes BayesTools_prior_region_mass_unavailable, BayesTools_prior_region_route_unavailable, BayesTools_prior_region_grid_unavailable, or BayesTools_prior_region_probability_rejected, all also BayesTools_hypothesis_region. Missing deterministic provenance for a region remains a metadata error, including in whole-factor tables. The specific BayesTools_transformation_image_unavailable leaf also produces an unavailable whole-factor row with its reason; other transformation and input errors remain strict. Scalar tests retain the original refusal. User-supplied prior draws (numeric or data-frame inputs without a prior object) have no structural prior density: their prior ordinate is the kernel (or normal) estimate of the prior expression draws, returned with a warning of classes BayesTools_inexact_ordinate and BayesTools_hypothesis_ordinate. Region tests require positive prior mass for every compared region. An implicit region statement is compared with its complement, which therefore also needs positive prior mass. Independently evaluated complements remain valid even when the other natural probability rounds to one. Explicit comparisons such as "theta > 0.5 vs theta > 0" accept an encompassing region with prior mass one. Rows are labelled by quantity; when several statements refer to the same quantity, the statement number is appended, e.g. theta (2). A call cannot combine statements that reference explicit levels of a factor (mu_fac[A] > 0) with statements that reference the whole factor (mu_fac = 0); it stops with an error naming the restriction, and the two kinds are evaluated in separate calls. A symbolic comparison on both sides uses its centered scalar expression: "theta = phi vs theta > phi" and "theta - phi = 0 vs theta - phi > 0" are supported. Reversed spelling "theta = phi vs phi < theta" remains conservatively unavailable; use the supported orientation or centered spelling. A reference to a quantity or level that posterior does not contain, and a parameter that it does not contain, stop with an error of class BayesTools_parameter_not_found (also BayesTools_parameter_resolution_error), as unresolved selectors of parameter_catalog_resolve() do; its fields alias and available name the unresolved and the available references.

Details

Level combinations require the same complete declared joint prior context. Fixed reference levels use the shared typed ordinate refusals; whole-factor requests retain results for eligible sibling levels. Region Bayes factors are calculated from their canonical log ratios even when intermediate diagnostic odds are outside the natural-scale range. A transitive ratio with both a numerically zero posterior point ordinate and zero posterior region mass is undefined and returns NA with a warning recorded in the result.

The hypothesis language deliberately accepts only a small, non-programmable subset of R expressions:


hypothesis := statement [ "vs" statement ]
statement  := point | region
point      := arithmetic ( "=" | "==" | "!=" ) finite_number
region     := relation
            | "(" region ")"
            | "!" region
            | region ( "&" | "|" ) region
relation   := arithmetic ( "<" | "<=" | ">" | ">=" ) arithmetic

Arithmetic expressions may contain parameter identifiers, finite numeric literals, parentheses, +, -, *, /, ^, and the one-argument functions abs(), exp(), log(), sqrt(), plogis(), and qlogis(). Every constant arithmetic subexpression must evaluate to one finite number. A point value may be one finite numeric literal, optionally preceded by one unary sign, or another parameter expression. Symbolic right-hand sides are normalized to a difference from zero. Relations with a constant on the left and a parameter expression on the right are normalized to the equivalent parameter-left form.

Equality defines a point hypothesis and may appear only as the top-level relation of a statement. It cannot be parenthesized inside, negated, or combined as a region. Region relations may be parenthesized, negated, and combined with the element-wise operators & and |; && and || are not supported. Backticks permit non-syntactic parameter names. In particular, escaped identifiers such as `Inf` refer to parameters, while unescaped Inf, NaN, NA, TRUE, and FALSE are reserved literals and are rejected. Whitespace-delimited vs (in any case) outside backticks is the separator word of a hypothesis, so a parameter named vs is written with backticks (`vs`), as hypothesis_render() writes it.

FormStatusReason
theta = -0.5acceptedpoint with a finite literal
theta = phiacceptednormalized to theta - phi = 0
0 > thetaacceptednormalized to theta < 0
(theta > 0)acceptedparenthesized region
!(theta > 0)acceptednegated region
theta > 0 & abs(phi) < 2acceptedcombined regions
`Inf` > 0acceptedescaped parameter identifier
!(theta == 0)rejectedpoint equalities cannot be negated
theta = 1 + 1rejectedconstant point value is not one literal
theta > 0 && phi < 1rejectedscalar boolean operator
sin(theta) > 0rejectedfunction outside the whitelist

Prior region masses of deterministic prior densities use the structure that prior_density_ordinate() classifies, for regions whose relations are linear in the quantity (e.g., theta > 0, 2 * theta < 1, and their combinations with &, |, and !): point masses contribute their exact probability, scalar and normal-sum priors their exact distribution functions, and Gaussian convolutions and conditional-normal scale mixtures the conditional-normal quadrature of the ordinate over the other term, split at the same breakpoints, with the Gaussian peak (where the ordinate uses one) at every finite region bound; mixture, model, and design-row components are summed with their probabilities. A quadrature that fails its diagnostics, or evaluates to exactly zero, stops with an error. Other prior densities and regions use the prior-density grid, which resolves the region boundaries on that grid: a boundary is located by bisection within each grid cell where the condition changes, but region features narrower than the grid spacing may be missed.

Affine expressions retain an unshifted linear numerator and a checked constant divisor. Point inference evaluates that numerator at the translated null; diagnostic density heights retain the requested quantity units. Numerical coefficient, boundary or log-ordinate resolution loss raises BayesTools_hypothesis_numerical_unavailable (ordinate parent) or BayesTools_hypothesis_region_numerical_unavailable (region parent), also BayesTools_numerical_unavailable and BayesTools_numerical_condition. The log-resolution screen is a conservative floating-point heuristic, not an estimator or backend error bound. Finite log values may correspond to displayed natural-scale zero or infinity. raw_log_BF and numerical_diagnostics retain aligned diagnostics; BF formatting uses the live column carrier, which replacement, arithmetic and Math operations invalidate. Supported scalar affine and Boolean regions use deterministic prior laws even when prior draws are available, as do regions over explicit factor levels whose comparisons are all of one linear combination of the levels (e.g., mu_fac[A] > mu_fac[B] + 0.5), which use the exact structural mass of that combination. Unsupported regions (nonlinear expressions or comparisons of different combinations, e.g., mu_fac[A] > 0 & mu_fac[B] > 0) retain their sampled route, or their existing no-draw grid route. Deterministic prior numerical diagnostics (method, absolute error and convergence when available) can be inspected with attr(result, "prior_numerical_diagnostics"); they are row-aligned through subsetting. BF_error remains Monte Carlo-only and omits prior Monte Carlo variance only for the actual deterministic route. Accepted positive scalar prior-region probabilities retain their backend log probabilities for canonical BF ratios, including positive subnormal masses. Natural zero or non-finite prior masses remain unavailable.

Data-frame coercion returns a plain long frame with leading component, parameter (the displayed row identity), and warning fields. Statistical values retain full precision. Bayes-factor names are BF10, BF01, logBF10, or logBF01 according to the displayed column attributes; BF_error retains its existing percent relative-error units. Declared nonmissing bounds are in BF_bound_operator. Unmatched/global warnings have component "hypothesis/warnings". Compact printing retains its existing layout. cbind() binds the displayed columns of hypothesis tables (with their row names, at full precision) into a plain data frame.

Fitted models

hypothesis_BF(fit, "(mu) cor = 0.9", BF01 = TRUE, seed = 1) tests the quantities of the parameter catalog (parameter_catalog()) of a fitted model by the names that JAGS_estimates_table() shows, without backticks (coefficients such as "x" or "x_fac[B]", random-effect quantities such as "(mu) sd(intercept)" or "(mu) cor", scalar parameters such as "sigma", and the total and the allocation shares of an ordered term, "f{total}" and "f[share: mid]", also by their earlier names "f_ordered_total" and "f_ordered_allocation[mid]"), and statements with vs work as for draws. The total of a spike-and-slab or mixture prior has a point mass at its null: its point tests need conditional = TRUE, and the total of a point prior is fixed by the model. On the original scale (transform_scaled = TRUE) a total is tested when the scaling leaves the coefficients of its term unchanged; the shares are unitless. A point null on a quantity with a prior point mass at that value (a spike-and-slab coefficient at its spike) stops with BayesTools_point_mass_at_null; conditional = TRUE tests the quantity within its inclusion event, and region hypotheses work without it. The fit method evaluates the Savage-Dickey density ratio (Dickey 1971; Wagenmakers et al. 2010) at the posterior and prior ordinates of the tested quantity; hypothesis_BF_model() describes the engine, its refusals, and the density backends that evaluate point hypotheses (hypothesis_density_backend()). The result is the same as extracting the quantity (parameter_mixed_posterior() or as_mixed_posteriors() with marginal_posterior()) and testing its draws.

References

Dickey JM (1971). “The weighted likelihood ratio, linear hypotheses on normal location parameters.” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 204–223. doi:10.1214/aoms/1177693507 .

Wagenmakers E, Lodewyckx T, Kuriyal H, Grasman R (2010). “Bayesian hypothesis testing for psychologists: A tutorial on the Savage-Dickey method.” Cognitive Psychology, 60(3), 158–189. doi:10.1016/j.cogpsych.2009.12.001 .
